title: Floor register: Proof strip
topics: Linked lists, binary trees and search trees
summary: Tree breadth-first traversal. Return the whole list.
descriptionMd:
Inputs
`root` is the top node of a binary tree. Examples list nodes one level at a time, from left to right. null marks a missing child; [] means no tree. Each node stores its number in val. Its left and right links point to children. The runner builds the nodes for you.

Your tasks
1. Create a list `levelSums`. `root` is the top node of a binary tree. Each node has a value and up to two children. The `root` is at depth 0, its children are at depth 1, and so on. Add the values at each depth. Put one sum per depth in `levelSums`, starting at depth 0. Missing children add nothing. An empty tree gives an empty `levelSums`.
2. Complete `floorRegisterProofStrip` so it returns `levelSums`. Return it, do not print it.

Example
If `root` is [7, null, 7, 3, -3], then `levelSums` is [7, 7, 0] and `floorRegisterProofStrip` returns [7, 7, 0].

Rules
- If `levelSums` is empty, return [].

Test data
TEST DATA 1: `root` is [4, null, 0, 13, -1].
TEST DATA 2: `root` is [2, null, 2, 2, -9].

Each problem in this unit builds `levelSums` first, then returns a different answer from it. Start with the first problem. The last problem also counts positions from 1.
constraints: 0 <= node count <= 31; null marks a missing child and does not count as a node.
Answers fit in a signed 32-bit integer: -2,147,483,648 through 2,147,483,647.
Input numbers have no decimal part. They range from -1,000,000 to 1,000,000. Follow any extra input rules in task 1.
Linked lists do not loop back to an earlier node. Tree examples list nodes by level; null means a missing child. The runner builds the nodes shown in the examples.
Efficiency goal: time O(n); extra memory, including the helper list, O(n). n is the number of nodes. These labels describe how work and memory grow with the input.
hints: Work through TEST DATA 1 by hand. Write down `levelSums` before you look for the answer.
